title: 🚀 Series A Founders' Journey
subtitle: From product-market fit to a $20M round in 6 quarters
theme: Lead a Series A SaaS startup through capital allocation, hiring, board, and crisis decisions
description: You are the CEO of Mentolytics, a $1M ARR analytics SaaS startup with 18 months of runway. The board wants $5M+ ARR and a Series A close inside 6 quarters. Each round you balance capital allocation, hiring, pricing, market expansion, and board management. Realistic financials, cap table dilution, market funnel, and stakeholder dynamics — all live.
learning_objectives: Allocate capital with hurdle rates, opportunity cost, and stop-loss criteria
Read P&L, unit economics, and runway as a coherent decision lens
Set vision with concrete milestones and explicit non-goals
Manage board alignment and term-sheet negotiation under pressure
Make calibrated decisions: pre-mortem, reversibility, confidence intervals

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Each round is one quarter. Read the dashboard (cap table, unit economics, board pulse).
Pick the option that best fits your strategy — every choice moves multiple dials.
Watch your runway. Crisis quarters give you only 2 minutes of decision time.
Close the Series A in Q6 with strong unit economics and an aligned board.
tips: LTV/CAC > 3 and payback < 18 months are table stakes for a Series A.
Burn multiple > 2 will frighten investors regardless of growth.
Don't dilute below 50% founder ownership unless you have a plan.

soundscape.description: R15 — VC office ambience + soft tactile cues for the Series A sim.

psychological_framework.description: Executive-tier dimensions: capital allocation, vision setting, governance judgment, talent strategy, commercial acumen, decision quality.

core_skills.name: Capital Allocation
core_skills.description: Choosing where each unit of capital earns the highest risk-adjusted return.

core_skills.name: Vision Setting
core_skills.description: Articulating a concrete 3-5y picture that aligns the team and forces trade-offs.

core_skills.name: Governance Judgment

core_skills.name: Talent Strategy
core_skills.description: Hiring, performance, comp, and culture on a 12-24 month horizon.

core_skills.name: Commercial Acumen

core_skills.name: Decision Quality
core_skills.description: Separating decision from outcome; calibrated confidence; pre-mortem.

llm_config.audience_default: Founder/CEO of a Series A SaaS startup, global market

scripted_moves.label: VC asks for monthly KPI letter
scripted_moves.narrative: Partner emails: 'send me the next 3 months of cohort data'.

hallmarks: Treats pricing as the highest-leverage lever at $1M ARR — not headcount
Hires for the next $5M, not the last $1M (growth marketer over brand-builder)
Discloses security incidents fully within 24h — trust > short-term cost
Negotiates term sheets — never signs the first one offered
Picks vertical focus over horizontal optionality at Series A
Doubles down on outbound when the funnel needs pricing fixed first
Hires a brand-builder at $230K + 0.5% before product-market fit
'Quietly fixes' a security incident without disclosing — board finds out
Signs the first term sheet because 'speed > marginal valuation'
Pivots to AI to chase a narrative instead of a thesis

rounds.title: Q1 — The Kickoff
rounds.scenario: ARR is $1M, growth has plateaued at 8% q/q for two quarters. Board wants a clear thesis for the next 18 months. Cash is $5M, monthly burn $280K. Where do you place your first big bet?
rounds.ai_image_prompt: A Series A founder in a modern startup office reviewing a strategy whiteboard with metrics and roadmap, confident and focused, semi-realistic illustration

choices.feedback: A pure growth bet. Watch your CAC and payback.
choices.label: Double outbound: hire 2 senior AEs, $40K/mo SDR program
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Hiring 2 senior AEs + an SDR program at 8% q/q growth is investing in a funnel that's already not converting. Fix conversion before scaling top-of-funnel.

choices.feedback: Long-cycle bet that pays off in NRR — if execution holds.
choices.label: Invest in platform: ship API, hire 3 engineers for 6 months
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Platform compounds — but only after you've validated pricing. Building API at $1M ARR is a 12-month project that delays the next raise.

choices.feedback: Pricing is the highest-leverage lever. Test elasticity carefully.
choices.label: Repackage pricing: move to per-seat with platform fee
choices.expert_rationale: At $1M ARR with 8% q/q growth, pricing is the single highest-leverage lever — bigger than headcount, bigger than feature work. Per-seat with platform fee captures NRR upside without burning cash.

choices.feedback: Optionality is real, but the clock is also real.
choices.label: Hold cash, run experiments for one quarter
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Optionality has a real cost: 90 days at 8% growth is 90 days of ARR you don't get back. Holding cash isn't a strategy; it's a deferral.

rounds.title: Q2 — Building the Team
rounds.scenario: Your VP Marketing seat is open. Three candidates: a brand-builder from a $30M ARR peer, a growth-marketer from a Series B fintech, and a senior IC who will need to grow into the role. Comp range $180K-$240K base.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Three diverse executive marketing candidates being interviewed in a startup boardroom, semi-realistic, professional

choices.feedback: Right hire if your bet is category creation.
choices.label: Hire the brand-builder ($230K + 0.5% equity)
choices.counterfactual_feedback: $230K + 0.5% equity for a brand-builder before PMF is the classic 'hired the right role at the wrong stage' mistake.

choices.feedback: Will move pipeline numbers in 90 days. May not build a brand.
choices.label: Hire the growth marketer ($210K + 0.4% equity)
choices.expert_rationale: At $1M ARR with a 5x growth target, you need a measurement-driven growth marketer — not a brand-builder. Brand is the right hire after $10M ARR; CAC science is the right hire now.

choices.feedback: Cheaper, loyal — high upside if they grow into it.
choices.label: Promote the senior IC (and pay $160K)
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Promoting an IC to VP is great for retention but rarely produces the 5x funnel science you need at this stage. Pair an external growth lead with an IC promo if budget allows.

choices.feedback: Open seats decay culture and pipeline.
choices.label: Leave the seat open another quarter
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Leaving the seat open another quarter means another quarter of Q1's plateau. The seat earns its salary in the first 60 days or it doesn't.

rounds.title: Q3 — Pricing Test Results
rounds.scenario: Your pricing test on 30 prospects shows: enterprise tier converts 40% lower at the new price, but ACV is up 60%. Sales is asking for a discount toolkit. CFO says hold the line.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Founder reviewing pricing dashboard with a sales leader and CFO, semi-realistic, modern boardroom

choices.feedback: Anchoring on value, not price. Hard but right.
choices.label: Hold the price; arm sales with ROI calculator instead

forecast_prompt.question: Forecast Q4 net new ARR growth (%). Provide an 80% CI.

forecast_capture.question: Forecast Q4 net new ARR growth (%). Provide an 80% CI.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Arming sales with an ROI calculator is a good move but doesn't address the 22% discount expectation in the data. You'll watch close rates drop.

choices.feedback: Speeds deals but trains the market on discounts.
choices.label: Allow up to 20% discounts via desk approval
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Approving up to 20% discounts via desk approval sets a price floor 20% below your sticker. You don't recover.

choices.feedback: Segment-aware pricing. Adds operational complexity.
choices.label: Split into Pro and Enterprise; keep Pro flat
choices.expert_rationale: Pro + Enterprise tiering preserves the price floor while letting Enterprise discount on volume. This is exactly how every successful SaaS handles the 'discount toolkit' temptation.

choices.feedback: Cheap to reverse, but you've now signaled you flinch.
choices.label: Roll back to old pricing
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Rolling back signals to your team that you don't have conviction. Pricing is a one-way door — own the move.

rounds.title: Q4 — Security Incident
rounds.scenario: 🚨 An engineer pushed a code change that leaked one customer's API keys publicly for 4 hours. No data accessed (yet). Press has not picked it up. You have 2 minutes to decide.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Founder in a war room with security team handling an incident, urgent atmosphere, semi-realistic

choices.feedback: Hard now, easier forever. Trust is your moat.
choices.label: Notify all affected customers + post a public incident report within 24h
choices.expert_rationale: Notify all affected customers + a public incident report within 24h is what founders who run public companies later in their career learn first. Cover-ups are how you lose your board.

choices.feedback: Defensible if disclosure obligations are narrow. Don't get caught.
choices.label: Notify the affected customer privately; rotate keys; no public post
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Private notification works when it's truly contained — but 'no public post' creates a paper trail that surfaces during your Series B due diligence.

choices.feedback: Delay invites a worse story.
choices.label: Wait for security audit results before notifying
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Waiting for an audit is a 2-week delay during which the breach gets disclosed by someone else. You don't control the narrative anymore.

choices.feedback: Career-defining downside. Don't.
choices.label: Quietly fix it and hope no one notices
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Cover-ups don't survive contact with reality — and when they unravel, you lose investor trust permanently. Career-ending move.

inbox_events.subject: Heard about the breach — comment?
inbox_events.body: I'm running a story tomorrow. On the record or off?

choices.label: On the record — get ahead of the narrative
No comment — let legal lead the response

rounds.title: Q5 — Term Sheet on the Table
rounds.scenario: Acme VC offers $20M Series A on $80M pre-money. 1x non-participating preferred. 1 board seat. Pool top-up to 12% pre-money. Standard protective provisions. You have a softer indication from a Tier-2 firm at $90M but slower.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Founder reviewing a term sheet across the table from an investor, careful negotiation atmosphere, semi-realistic

choices.feedback: Lead quality matters more than 12% on pre-money.
choices.label: Sign Acme: speed > marginal valuation
choices.counterfactual_feedback: 'Speed > marginal valuation' is a story founders tell themselves to avoid the discomfort of negotiation. The marginal valuation isn't marginal at Series A — it's 15% of your cap table.

choices.feedback: Modest ask, big dilution impact. Most leads accept.
choices.label: Push back: $85M pre-money, pool top-up post-money
choices.expert_rationale: Pushing back on Acme for $85M pre-money + post-money pool top-up is the standard negotiation move. First offers are starting points; founders who don't negotiate leave 15-20% on the table.

choices.feedback: Risky if Acme walks. Brand damage if mishandled.
choices.label: Use Acme to bring Tier-2 to a hard offer
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Using Acme to bring Tier-2 to a hard offer can work — but it's a high-variance play. Done badly, you lose Acme too.

choices.feedback: Optionality preserved. Burn clock loud now.
choices.label: Decline; raise a smaller bridge instead
choices.counterfactual_feedback: A bridge round at this stage signals you couldn't get terms done. Lead investors talk.

live_investor.investor_persona: Maya Iyer, senior partner at Acme Ventures. Direct, data-driven, won't let founders coast on optimism. Has led 14 Series A rounds; her firm walks 30% of the time at this stage.
investor_goals: Lock the deal on Acme's published terms (12% pool top-up pre-money, 1x non-participating preferred)
Probe the founder's grasp of dilution math vs. valuation theatre
Test conviction — push on the Tier-2 alternative as a bluff
investor_constraints: Cannot offer board observer + voting board seat (only one)
$80M pre-money is firm absent material new diligence
Will respect a clean negotiated counter; will exit on amateur posturing
founder_goals: Defend valuation without burning the relationship
Trade structural concessions (esop timing, board) for headline price
Show command of pre-money/post-money + dilution arithmetic

pvp_mode.label: Live PvP — negotiate against another player

roles.label: Founder/CEO
roles.objective: Defend pre-money valuation without burning the relationship. Trade structural concessions (esop timing, board) for headline price.
roles.starting_position: $85M pre-money, post-money pool top-up, 1 board seat
roles.info_asymmetry: You know your runway, churn cohorts, and the soft Tier-2 indication.

roles.label: Lead Investor (Acme VC)
roles.objective: Lock the round at $80M pre-money with 12% pool top-up pre-money. Probe whether the founder is bluffing on Tier-2.
roles.starting_position: $80M pre-money, 12% pool top-up pre-money, 1 board seat, 1x non-participating preferred
roles.info_asymmetry: You know Acme's prior portfolio comps and walk rate. You don't know if Tier-2 is real.

founder: Concedes pool top-up timing without losing valuation: +governance_judgment

rounds.title: Q6 — The Year-End Read
rounds.scenario: 12 months in. ARR is $3.2M (3.2x), GM 76%, payback 14mo, NRR 116%, runway 22mo. Board wants a 3-year vision. Articulate the next bet — and what you will explicitly NOT do.
rounds.ai_image_prompt: Founder presenting a 3-year strategy on stage to investors and team, confident and grounded, semi-realistic

choices.feedback: A real thesis with non-goals. Disagreeable in the right way.
choices.label: Vertical SaaS thesis: own healthcare; explicitly skip retail and edtech
choices.expert_rationale: Vertical SaaS thesis (own healthcare, skip retail/edtech) is the move that compounds. Series A is when you commit to a thesis — horizontal platforms work at $20M ARR, not $5M.

choices.feedback: Less wrong than a slogan, but still no non-goals.
choices.label: Horizontal analytics platform; let market pull us
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Letting the market pull you horizontal at Series A is how you end up doing five things badly instead of one thing well.

choices.feedback: High-conviction, high-cost. Where's your evidence?
choices.label: Pivot to AI-native analytics; rebuild over 2 quarters
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Pivoting to 'AI-native analytics' to chase a narrative is the kind of move that funds the round and kills the company.

choices.feedback: Banal in a board memo, but not always wrong.
choices.label: Triple down on what's working; revisit thesis next year
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Tripling down on what's working is fine — but 'revisit thesis next year' means another year of avoiding the focus question.

endings.title: 🎉 Series A Closed
endings.summary: You closed a $20M Series A on solid unit economics. Now the real work begins.

endings.title: 🌉 Bridge Round
endings.summary: You raised $5M in bridge financing. Two more quarters to prove the thesis.

endings.title: 📉 Down Round
endings.summary: Term sheet at $40M pre-money. Painful dilution. Survive and learn.

coaching_moment: Most founders confuse decision quality with outcome quality. A great Series A is built on a hundred boring, calibrated, reversible bets — and the courage to pre-commit to kill criteria on the irreversible ones.
reflection_prompt: Which of your 6 choices was your highest-leverage decision — and was it Type 1 (irreversible) or Type 2 (reversible)?

glossary_terms.definition: Annual Recurring Revenue — the contractual revenue value of your subscription business, normalized to a year.
Net cash burned ÷ net new ARR added in a period. Below 1 is exceptional; above 2 spooks investors.
Lifetime value of a customer divided by cost to acquire them. > 3 is healthy for SaaS.
Net Revenue Retention. Revenue from existing customers (incl. expansion, churn) vs. one year ago, as a %. >110% is great.
Pre-money is company valuation before new investment; post-money = pre-money + new investment. New investor's % = investment / post-money.
Employee Stock Option Pool — shares set aside for current and future employee equity grants.
Non-binding outline of the economic and control terms of a financing round.
